position.title: The right AI starts with three questions.

pillars.label: Where
pillars.text: In the processes that cost you the most time, errors, or money.

pillars.label: How
pillars.text: With your team and the tools you already have, so they learn to do it themselves.

pillars.label: What for
pillars.text: Results you can measure: hours saved, fewer errors, faster responses.

statement: It's not about using AI everywhere. It's about using it where it changes the results.

problem.title: What we see
problem.lead: We talk with companies that were quoted a very high price for an AI system. The work underneath was repetitive: it could be automated, and the team could learn to maintain it.

items.title: A system priced far above the problem.
items.text: A custom platform gets proposed when the case is an email, a report, or an answer that already exists somewhere.

items.title: The repetitive work stays with the team.
items.text: Email, reports, copying data between systems, answering the same questions. That is where AI applies, and where it can be automated.

items.title: The team is left depending on whoever sold it.
items.text: If only the vendor knows how the system works, every change costs again. The solution has to stay with the company.

outcomes.title: The results we aim for
outcomes.lead: We don't promise an abstract transformation. We look for a few processes where AI shows up in the week.

items.title: Fewer hours on repetitive work
items.text: Email, reports, and moving data stop occupying the people who should be making decisions.

items.title: Fewer handoff errors
items.text: When information is no longer copied by hand, rework and last-minute reconciliations drop.

items.title: Faster answers
items.text: Customers, prospects, and employees get a consistent answer without waiting for the person who has it in their head.

items.title: A team that can carry on
items.text: We document, leave templates, and train the people who will maintain what we build.

approach.title: How we think about the work
approach.lead: We have spent more than 25 years building software, and the last year building AI agents and training teams at large companies. That combination changes the advice: we know where AI changes the results, and when automating what you already have is enough.

items.title: We start from the operation
items.text: We interview the people who do the work. If a process doesn't hurt every week, it is not the first one.

items.title: We stay vendor-neutral
items.text: We use what the company already has. We don't sell licenses or push a platform.

items.title: We teach while we build
items.text: The solution stays with the team. If three months later only we know how it works, the work was done wrong.

items.title: We will say no
items.text: If the process is repetitive, we don't build a custom system. We automate it with what you already have. If AI isn't justified, we say that too.

why.title: Why SmartMark
why.lead: Anyone can sell you AI. We tell you where you need it, how to apply it so it works, and what results to expect. And where you don't need it.

items.title: Real experience
items.text: We have spent more than 25 years building software companies actually use, and the last year building AI agents and training teams at large companies. That combination avoids two mistakes: proposing something that cannot be built, and building something the team will not use.

items.title: Vendor-neutral
items.text: We recommend what the company already has, or what the case justifies. We don't sell licenses and we don't push a platform. If the right tool is one you already pay for, the project starts there.

items.title: We teach, not create dependency
items.text: The work is documented, with templates and with the people who will maintain it. If three months later only we know how it works, the engagement was done wrong. The aim is that your team can carry on.

items.title: Built around how your company works
items.text: We work in Spanish and English, with the way most companies actually operate: lean teams, several tools at once, and budgets that have to earn their place. The solution is designed for that context, not for an office that isn't yours.

cases.title: AI use cases by business area
cases.lead: This is where AI usually makes a difference first: work that repeats, eats up hours, and can be improved with the tools you already pay for.

items.title: Customer service
items.text: What comes in again and again stops taking the people who should be on the difficult cases.
items.situation: The team answers the same questions by email, chat, and phone. The right answer lives in a manual, in an email from months ago, or in the head of the person who has been there longest. Meanwhile, the case that actually needs judgment waits.
builds: An assistant loaded with the company's documents, tone, and rules, to draft the first reply.
A sort of what comes in: the repeated items get an answer or a suggestion, and the sensitive ones go to a person with the context already assembled.
Ready prompts for the replies people currently write from scratch.
items.keeps: The team knows which documents feed the assistant and how to correct it when a policy changes. A person still handles the cases that matter.

items.title: Sales
items.text: Following up a lead and drafting a proposal no longer wait for someone to have a free afternoon.
items.situation: A prospect writes, the details stay in one person's inbox, and the proposal is built by copying the last one. What gets lost is not a tool. It is the day someone needed an answer.
builds: A follow-up that prepares the next message from the prospect's history and the company's offer.
A first draft of a proposal from a template, the client's details, and what was already discussed.
A summary of the call or the email, so the rest of the team can pick it up without asking what was said.
items.keeps: The templates and prompts stay with the sales team. They adjust the tone. They don't wait for an outsider to rewrite every proposal.

items.title: Finance
items.text: Someone stops reading the whole batch. They review the exceptions.
items.situation: Invoices, receipts, and spreadsheets are matched by hand across email, the bank, and the accounting system. The error doesn't show up in the total. It shows up in the line someone copied wrong on a Friday.
builds: Invoice and receipt reading that pulls vendor, amount, date, and tax into a format the system already accepts.
A reconciliation that flags what doesn't match and lets the rest through.
A check for what's missing: incomplete documents, or vendors that don't match the master list.
items.keeps: A person still approves. The difference is that they approve exceptions, instead of retyping the batch.

items.title: Human resources
items.text: A first reading of candidates, and clear answers to what employees ask every week.
items.situation: Resumes are read one by one against a job description that lives in a document. At the same time, employees ask about leave, policy, and benefits, and the answer depends on who is free.
builds: A first reading that compares candidates with the criteria for the role and leaves a note. It does not make the decision.
Answers to the internal questions that come up often, using the current policy, and a clear path for anything a machine should not answer.
Drafts of job descriptions and messages to candidates, in the company's voice.
items.keeps: Hiring stays a person's decision. The assistant does not reject anyone on its own, and the team knows which criteria it is using.

items.title: Operations
items.text: The report someone assembles by hand comes from the sources, not from a fresh spreadsheet.
items.situation: The numbers live in email, in a sheet, in the inventory system, and in a supplier's message. One person pulls them together before the meeting. If that person is out, the report doesn't exist.
builds: A report that takes those sources and leaves them in the format the meeting already uses.
Alerts when a figure didn't arrive, or when a number sits outside the usual range.
A short guide so someone else on the team can change a source or a column without starting over.
items.keeps: The report stops belonging to one person. Where each figure comes from is written down.

items.title: Management
items.text: A usable summary of meetings, documents, and indicators, before the next decision.
items.situation: The decision waits while someone reads the thread, the notes, and three dashboards. What matters is mixed in with what was already decided last week.
builds: A meeting summary with decisions, owners, and what was left open.
A reading of long documents — contracts, reports, policies — aimed at the questions management has already been asking.
A short brief on the indicators: what moved, what didn't arrive, and what deserves a conversation, without replacing the dashboard.
items.keeps: Management still decides. They get the material in order, and the team knows how to ask for the next summary.
